title: Okaikoi and the Power of the Sun

pages.text: Okaikoi’s family had a small solar lamp. Each morning, he put it in the sun on the window sill. At night, it gave light for his homework. “How does the sun make our lamp shine at night?” he asked.
sentences: Okaikoi’s family had a small solar lamp.
Each morning, he put it in the sun on the window sill.
At night, it gave light for his homework.
“How does the sun make our lamp shine at night?” he asked.
pages.alt: In golden morning sunlight, Okaikoi places a compact yellow solar lantern with a small dark solar panel on top onto a sunny wooden window sill.

pages.text: His teacher said, “The lamp has a small panel. The panel takes in energy from the sun. It turns the energy into electricity. A battery keeps the electricity. At night, the battery gives light.”
sentences: His teacher said, “The lamp has a small panel.
The panel takes in energy from the sun.
It turns the energy into electricity.
A battery keeps the electricity.
At night, the battery gives light.”
pages.alt: In the classroom, the teacher points to the dark solar panel on top of Okaikoi’s yellow solar lamp on the desk while Okaikoi and Nafisa look closely.

pages.text: Nafisa knew another source. “At Akosombo, a big dam holds back the Volta River. Water flows through machines and turns them. The machines make electricity.” “Water makes electricity, too!” said Okaikoi.
sentences: Nafisa knew another source.
“At Akosombo, a big dam holds back the Volta River.
Water flows through machines and turns them.
The machines make electricity.” “Water makes electricity, too!” said Okaikoi.
pages.alt: Nafisa holding up a vivid wordless painting of the wide concrete Akosombo Dam holding back blue Lake Volta with white water rushing below through green hills.

pages.text: The teacher named more ways. “Gas can make electricity when it burns. Wind can make it, too. The sun, water and wind will not run out.” The children wrote a list.
sentences: The teacher named more ways.
“Gas can make electricity when it burns.
Wind can make it, too.
The sun, water and wind will not run out.” The children wrote a list.
pages.alt: On the classroom board hang four simple wordless picture cards showing a bright sun, a flowing river dam, a blue gas flame and a white wind turbine.

pages.text: Then the teacher spoke firmly. “Electricity helps us, but it can hurt us. Never touch bare wires or a fallen wire. Never put things into a socket. Never touch a switch with wet hands. Keep away from power poles, and never fly a kite near power lines.”
sentences: Then the teacher spoke firmly.
“Electricity helps us, but it can hurt us.
Never touch bare wires or a fallen wire.
Never put things into a socket.
Never touch a switch with wet hands.
Keep away from power poles, and never fly a kite near power lines.”
pages.alt: The teacher raising one finger seriously in class beside wordless safety picture icons showing a crossed-out wall socket and wet hands away from a switch.

pages.text: “If you see a fallen wire or a broken socket, stay far away and tell a grown-up at once,” she said. Okaikoi nodded. At home, he told his little brother the rules. Then they set the lamp out in the warm sun.
sentences: “If you see a fallen wire or a broken socket, stay far away and tell a grown-up at once,” she said.
Okaikoi nodded.
At home, he told his little brother the rules.
Then they set the lamp out in the warm sun.
pages.alt: At home, Okaikoi gently guides his younger brother back from a wall socket while pointing toward the yellow solar lamp resting safely on the sunny sill.
